text: By the early 1960s the university looked south, across the Midway, toward Woodlawn.

Woodlawn was a densely populated, mostly Black neighborhood, and the university began planning a South Campus expansion into it, talking about clearing a strip roughly a block deep, the land between 60th and 61st Streets, just south of the Midway.
It used the same playbook, announcing it would spend its own millions to trigger a much larger federal grant.
A sociologist dismissed the area in print as a community that reads nothing.
It was the kind of contempt that had gone unanswered in Hyde Park.
But Woodlawn pushed back in a way Hyde Park's displaced never could.
Residents, block clubs, and pastors, led by a minister named Arthur Brazier and helped by the organizer Saul Alinsky, built The Woodlawn Organization, known as TWO.
Brazier told the university that Woodlawn was not its private colony.
TWO fought the expansion through the early sixties, and in 1964 it won a written agreement.
The university would get its South Campus land, but it agreed not to expand south of 61st Street, and the deal required new low and moderate income housing be built in Woodlawn as part of it.
For the first time, the university had to negotiate with the neighborhood it wanted to remake instead of simply planning over it.
That line at 61st Street held for decades.
The lesson of Hyde Park was carved into the map.
North of the line, the university rebuilt a neighborhood and decided who came back.
South of it, an organized community drew a border and made the university stop.
Both of those facts are still on the ground today, in the towers on 55th Street and in the line at 61st.
